one_liner: A single-threaded, `?Send` agent turn loop (`AgentLoop`) that alternates call-model / run-tools — batching consecutive read-only tool calls concurrently, serializing writes, enforcing a model/tool-call budget, polling a cancel closure, routing image turns to a separate vision provider, and re-selecting the per-turn tool schema view from `tool_search` hints + lexical scoring.
how_it_works: `AgentLoop::run_turn` takes the event sink out of `&mut self` (to dodge a borrow conflict between the sink closure and `&mut self`), runs `run_turn_inner`, then applies the Stop hook and restores the sink. Inner: it sets `use_vision_this_turn` if a vision provider exists AND the user content carries an `image_url` block (`has_image_block`), fires the `user_prompt` hook (which can short-circuit the whole turn with stop_reason `blocked`), appends the user message, then iterates `for iteration in 0..max_model_calls` where `max_model_calls = max_iterations.min(task_budget.max_model_calls.max(1))`. Each iteration: checks the cancel closure; rebuilds the tool schema list via `schemas_for_query(tool_query)` (so `tool_search` hits surface next turn); prepends a synthetic system `budget_note` plus any prompt-hook output; calls `call_model`, which first builds a non-destructive context-edited message view (`Session::for_model_edited`) then dispatches to `active_provider()` (vision or main). On `finish_reason=="error"` it returns an error TurnResult; on no tool calls it records the assistant text and returns `completed`; otherwise it persists the assistant message with OpenAI-shaped `tool_calls` and walks `response.tool_calls` by index. For each position it re-checks cancel and remaining tool budget, then decides `parallel_run`: true only when the current AND next call are both `read_only` per the registry — it then greedily gathers the maximal run of consecutive read-only calls (capped by remaining budget) and runs them via `join_all` over `execute_cancellable`; otherwise it runs the single (write/unknown) call serially. Results are appended in original order with `add_tool_result(id, name, result)`. Falling out of the model-call loop yields stop_reason `task_budget`. The `ToolRegistry::execute` dispatches by name (unknown name → an error string fed back to the model), running pre/post hooks around the tool.
design_rationale: The defining constraint is `#[async_trait(?Send)]` on the `Provider`, `Tool`, and `ApprovalHandler` traits: the whole agent is built to run on a Tokio current-thread runtime so it can hold non-`Send` state — `Rc<RefCell<…>>` shared context (the plan, tool catalog, tool hints), boxed `FnMut` mock/closure providers in tests, and the GUI's `FnMut` event sink — without the `Send + Sync + 'static` tax that a multi-threaded runtime forces (which would push everything to `Arc<Mutex<…>>` and atomic refcounts). The work is I/O-bound (one in-flight model call, then a short burst of tool I/O), so multi-threading buys nothing; the read-only batch concurrency is achieved with `join_all` of futures on one thread, not OS threads, so `Send` is never needed. Read-only-only batching is the safety rationale: pure-read tools have no ordering dependency and can race freely, but a write (or unknown) tool must stay serial and in declared order so file edits and their surrounding reads observe a deterministic sequence (verified by `write_between_reads_stays_serial_and_ordered`). The dual budget (model calls vs tool calls) plus a self-describing `budget_note` injected as a system message lets the model self-pace and guarantees termination even if it loops; backfilling synthetic tool results on cancel/budget keeps the message history API-valid (every assistant tool_call must have a matching tool reply or the next request 400s). Dynamic per-turn schema selection (cap `DEFAULT_VISIBLE_TOOL_LIMIT=9`, always-visible core set + `tool_search` hints + lexical matches) keeps the prompt small and the function list focused as the tool set grows, rejecting the alternative of dumping every schema every turn.

key_mechanisms.name: !Send / current-thread design
key_mechanisms.detail: `#[async_trait(?Send)]` on `Provider`/`Tool`/`ApprovalHandler` means returned futures need not be `Send`. This lets `Box<dyn Provider>`, the `EventSink = Box<dyn FnMut(LoopEvent)>`, and `Rc<RefCell<…>>` shared state live across awaits on a single-thread runtime. Rationale: I/O-bound workload + cheap `Rc` sharing; rejected `Arc<Mutex>`/`Send` bounds as unnecessary overhead.

key_mechanisms.name: call-model → run-tools iteration
key_mechanisms.detail: `run_turn_inner` loops up to `max_model_calls`. Each pass: `call_model` (schemas + budget/hook system notes) → if `!response.has_tool_calls()` return `completed`; else persist assistant `tool_calls` and execute them, append results, loop. Falling off the end returns `task_budget`.

key_mechanisms.name: tool-call parse + dispatch
key_mechanisms.detail: The provider crate parses raw JSON into `ToolCall{id,name,arguments}` (invalid/non-object arguments collapse to `{}`, per types.rs). The loop re-serializes them to OpenAI `function` shape for history, then dispatches by name through `ToolRegistry::execute`; an unknown name returns `Error: unknown tool '<name>'.` back to the model rather than crashing.

key_mechanisms.name: concurrent read-only batching
key_mechanisms.detail: `parallel_run` triggers only when `is_read_only(calls[idx])` AND `is_read_only(calls[idx+1])`. It greedily collects the maximal run of consecutive read-only calls (bounded by `remaining_tools`), runs them with `futures_util::future::join_all` over `execute_cancellable`, and zips results back in order. A non-read-only or trailing single call runs serially. Proven by `read_only_calls_run_concurrently` (4×300ms reads finish <800ms).

key_mechanisms.name: task budget (dual cap)
key_mechanisms.detail: `TaskBudget{max_model_calls:60, max_tool_calls:120}` (defaults). `max_model_calls` caps the outer loop; before each tool/batch, `remaining_tools = max_tool_calls.saturating_sub(tools_used.len())` — 0 → `budget_result` (stop_reason `task_budget`, backfill unanswered). A `budget_note` system message reports live usage so the model paces itself.

key_mechanisms.name: cancellation
key_mechanisms.detail: `run_turn` takes an `Option<&dyn Fn()->bool>`. Checked at loop top, before each tool/batch, and after each tool. `execute_cancellable` `tokio::select!`s the tool future (biased) against a 100ms poll; if cancel flips mid-run it returns `[interrupted...]` and drops (cancels) the tool future. `stop_interrupts_a_hanging_tool` proves a `pending()` tool is abandoned.

key_mechanisms.name: vision routing
key_mechanisms.detail: `use_vision_this_turn = vision_provider.is_some() && has_image_block(user_input)`. `active_provider()` returns the vision provider for that turn only; absent a vision provider, image turns stay on the main provider. `has_image_block` scans the content array for a block whose `type == "image_url"`.

key_mechanisms.name: dynamic per-turn schema selection
key_mechanisms.detail: Each iteration calls `schemas_for_query(tool_query)`. If `tools.len() <= 9` all schemas are sent; otherwise the view = `ALWAYS_VISIBLE_TOOLS` (read_file, apply_patch, update_plan, shell, tool_search, skill) + names in `ctx.tool_hints` (set by the last `tool_search`) + top lexical matches via `catalog_score`, capped at the limit. `tool_search` populates `tool_hints` so a discovered tool's schema appears next turn.

key_mechanisms.name: non-destructive context editing
key_mechanisms.detail: `call_model` runs `Session::for_model_edited(notes, policy)` which builds a send-time view: compresses old (`tool`) results beyond `keep_recent_messages` to `max_tool_result_chars`, and drops the oldest prefix (re-aligned to a user boundary) when over `max_chars` — without mutating `session.messages`. Trace prints original/edited chars + compressed/dropped counts.

interview_talking_points: Why `?Send` is the load-bearing decision: the agent is I/O-bound and runs on a current-thread Tokio runtime, so it can share state with `Rc<RefCell>` and hold `FnMut`/mock providers across awaits — no `Send+Sync+'static`, no `Arc<Mutex>`. Concurrency where it matters (parallel reads) is single-thread `join_all`, not OS threads.

Read-only batching is correctness-driven, not just speed: only a run of *consecutive* read-only calls is parallelized; any write or unknown tool forces serial, in-order execution so edits and the reads around them are deterministic. The batch is also clipped to the remaining tool budget.

Two independent budgets (model calls and tool calls) guarantee termination and are surfaced to the model as a live system `budget_note`, turning a hard limit into self-pacing guidance; exhaustion backfills synthetic tool replies so history stays API-valid.

Cancellation is cooperative and two-layered: a `Fn()->bool` polled at loop/tool boundaries, plus `execute_cancellable`'s 100ms `select!` that can abandon a hanging tool mid-run by dropping its future (test uses `future::pending`).

Dynamic per-turn tool schema selection (cap 9, always-visible core + `tool_search` hints + lexical scoring) keeps the function list small as tools grow; `tool_search` writes into `ctx.tool_hints` so a discovered tool becomes visible next turn — a feedback loop between a tool's side effect and the next prompt.
Vision routing is per-turn and opt-in: only when a separate vision provider is configured AND the turn carries an `image_url` block, keeping a cheaper text model as the default.

Robustness of message history: unknown tool names return an error string (not a panic), context editing is a non-destructive send-time view, and cancel/budget paths backfill dangling tool_calls so the OpenAI invariant (every tool_call has a tool reply) is never violated.
tradeoffs_or_gotchas: Cancellation granularity is 100ms (the `execute_cancellable` poll); a tool that returns faster than the first poll cannot be interrupted, and there's no hard wall-clock timeout in the loop itself (per-tool timeouts live in the `shell` tool, not the harness).
Read-only batching keys entirely on the registry's `read_only()` flag; a tool mis-declared read-only (one that actually mutates) would be raced and reordered. Trust boundary is the tool author.

`with_max_iterations` overwrites `task_budget.max_model_calls`, and `with_task_budget` overwrites `max_iterations`; the two setters clobber each other depending on call order — the effective cap is always `max_iterations.min(max_model_calls.max(1))`, so a mismatched pair can silently lower the cap.

The tool-call budget is checked *before* each call/batch, so a parallel read-only batch is sized to fit the remaining budget but the loop never partially runs a batch beyond it — fine, but it means a single over-budget assistant turn truncates remaining calls and backfills them as 'task budget exhausted'.
Vision routing is all-or-nothing per turn: a turn with an image sends the *entire* edited history to the vision provider, not just the image; there's no per-message model split.
Tool-call argument parsing is delegated to the provider crate — invalid/non-object JSON collapses to `{}` there, so a malformed arguments blob silently becomes empty rather than erroring at dispatch.

Schema selection lexical scoring (`catalog_score`) is a simple substring/word match (name exact=100, name-contains=50, hay-contains=20); a capability described in synonyms the query doesn't share won't surface unless `tool_search` is called explicitly.

subsystem: context-compression (context editing / session history shaping) in ncx-core's Session — D:/agent_prac/ncx-train/rust/crates/ncx-core/src/session.rs
one_liner: A two-mode context editor: every model call gets a non-destructive, budget-shaped "provider view" (truncate old tool results, then drop the oldest message prefix past a char budget), while an opt-in /compact bakes that same transform into the live history and rewrites the JSONL log.
how_it_works: Session stores the full conversation as Vec<serde_json::Value> in OpenAI chat shape (`messages`), with the system prompt held separately in `system`. ContextEditPolicy carries four knobs: `enabled`, `max_chars` (default 120_000), `keep_recent_messages` (default 30), `max_tool_result_chars` (default 4_000). The core algorithm lives in `edited_body(system_notes, policy)`: it clones `self.messages` into `body`, records `original_chars` via `total_chars` (chars of system + notes + every message serialized to JSON), then if `policy.enabled` runs two passes. Pass 1 (tool-result shrink): compute `recent_cutoff = body.len() - keep_recent_messages` (saturating), and for every message at index `i < recent_cutoff` whose role is "tool", call `compress_tool_result`, which truncates the `content` string to the first `max_tool_result_chars` chars and appends a marker `\n[context edited: omitted the rest of prior {name} result; original_chars=N]`, returning true so `stats.compressed_tool_results` increments. Pass 2 (prefix drop): only if `total_chars(...) > max_chars` AND `body.len() > keep_recent_messages`, set `start = body.len() - keep_recent_messages`, then advance `start` to the first "user" message at/after that cutoff (`position(role==user)`), then skip any leading "tool" messages, and if `0 < start < body.len()` set `dropped_messages = start` and keep only `body[start..]`. `for_model_edited` then prepends the system message and any non-empty `system_notes` as extra system messages, appends the edited body, and reports `edited_chars`. `for_model` is just `for_model_edited(&[], policy{enabled:false})`. `compact` reuses `edited_body` with `enabled` forced true and, only if something actually changed (compressed or dropped > 0), overwrites `self.messages` and calls `rewrite_log` to truncate-and-rewrite the JSONL file. The send-time view is wired in agent_loop.rs `call_model`, which calls `for_model_edited(system_notes, &self.context_edit)` before every provider `chat`; the destructive `/compact` path is the CLI's `compact_session_text` calling `agent.session.compact`.
design_rationale: The central design choice is non-destructive send-time editing: `for_model_edited` builds a temporary trimmed view and leaves `self.messages` (the canonical log) untouched, so the full transcript is always preserved for `--resume` and the JSONL log even though the model only ever sees a budget-bounded slice. The test `context_edit_compresses_old_tool_results_without_mutating_session` asserts exactly this (session keeps the 200-char original). The two passes are deliberately ordered cheap-then-expensive: tool-result truncation runs first because verbose tool outputs (shell dumps, file reads) are the dominant, lowest-value bulk in a coding agent's history, so shrinking them often gets back under budget without losing any conversational turns; only if that is insufficient does it resort to dropping whole messages. The prefix-drop is conservative: it always keeps `keep_recent_messages`, and rather than cutting at an arbitrary index it advances the cut to a "user" boundary and skips leading orphan "tool" messages — this preserves the OpenAI invariant that the history starts cleanly and that no "tool" message is left without its preceding assistant tool_call (a malformed prefix would be rejected by the API). `compact` is opt-in and only mutates/rewrites when work was actually done (the `compress > 0 || dropped > 0` guard), so a no-op compact under budget leaves the log byte-identical (test `compact_noops_when_under_budget`). Char-counting (`json_chars` on serialized JSON, counting Unicode scalars via `.chars().count()`) is a deliberately cheap proxy for token budget — it avoids a tokenizer dependency, trading exactness for a fast, provider-agnostic heuristic. Truncation uses `.chars().take(n)` rather than byte slicing to avoid panicking on a multi-byte UTF-8 boundary.

key_mechanisms.name: ContextEditPolicy

Defaults in both session.rs Default impl and ncx-config; CLI builds it via context_edit_from_config with positive_usize fallbacks, so a non-positive config value silently falls back to the default.

key_mechanisms.name: edited_body (the algorithm)
key_mechanisms.detail: Two-pass, char-budget-driven. Pass 1 compresses tool results older than the recent window; pass 2 drops the oldest prefix only when total_chars > max_chars and there are more than keep_recent_messages. Returns (body, ContextEditStats).

key_mechanisms.name: compress_tool_result
key_mechanisms.detail: In-place mutation of a 'tool' message: if content chars > max_chars, replace content with head(max_chars) + a '[context edited: ... original_chars=N]' marker so the model knows truncation happened. Returns bool to drive the compressed_tool_results counter.

key_mechanisms.name: for_model_edited (non-destructive view)
key_mechanisms.detail: Prepends system + non-empty system_notes (each as its own system message), then the edited body. Used on every turn via AgentLoop::call_model. Leaves self.messages intact.

key_mechanisms.name: compact (destructive materialization)
key_mechanisms.detail: Forces enabled=true, runs edited_body, and only if it changed anything overwrites self.messages and rewrite_log()s the JSONL — so /compact and subsequent --resume see the compacted history, not just a temporary view.

key_mechanisms.name: prefix-drop boundary safety
key_mechanisms.detail: start begins at len-keep_recent, advances to the first 'user' message, then skips leading 'tool' messages, guarding against an orphaned tool reply at the head of the trimmed history (OpenAI shape invariant).

key_mechanisms.name: ContextEditStats
key_mechanisms.detail: original_chars / edited_chars / compressed_tool_results / dropped_messages — surfaced to the user by /compact as 'chars X -> Y; compressed_tool_results=..; dropped_messages=..'.

key_mechanisms.name: resume / log integrity
key_mechanisms.detail: Log is append-only JSONL with _ts stamps and inline base64 images redacted (redact_image_data). resume() reads the log, drops system rows, and sanitize_restored_messages backfills synthetic '[interrupted...]' tool replies for any dangling tool_call so resumed history is API-valid.

flow_steps: AgentLoop::call_model is invoked for a turn and calls session.for_model_edited(system_notes, &self.context_edit).
edited_body clones self.messages into body and records original_chars = total_chars(system, notes, messages).

If policy.enabled: Pass 1 computes recent_cutoff = len - keep_recent_messages and for each older 'tool' message calls compress_tool_result (truncate to max_tool_result_chars + edit marker), counting compressed_tool_results.
Still in Pass 2: if total_chars(after compression) > max_chars AND len > keep_recent_messages, compute start = len - keep_recent_messages.
Advance start to the first 'user' message at/after the cutoff, then skip any leading 'tool' messages to keep the prefix API-valid.
If 0 < start < len, set dropped_messages = start and slice body = body[start..].
Set edited_chars and return (body, stats).
for_model_edited prepends the system message + each non-empty system_note as system messages, appends body, recomputes edited_chars over the serialized output, and returns ContextMessages.
call_model sends edited.messages to the provider's chat(); self.messages is never mutated by this path.

Separately, on /compact the CLI calls session.compact(policy): same edited_body with enabled forced true; if anything changed, self.messages is overwritten and rewrite_log truncates+rewrites the JSONL so resume sees the compacted history.
interview_talking_points: The headline distinction: send-time view (for_model_edited, every turn, non-destructive) vs. materialized compaction (compact, opt-in via /compact, rewrites the log). The full transcript is the source of truth; the model sees a budget-bounded projection of it.
Cheap-before-expensive ordering: shrink verbose tool results first (the bulk in a coding agent), drop whole messages only if still over budget. This minimizes conversational loss.
Why char counts not tokens: json_chars/total_chars use serialized-JSON Unicode-scalar counts as a tokenizer-free, provider-agnostic budget proxy — exactness traded for speed and zero dependencies.

API-shape invariants drive the drop logic: keep_recent floor, cut at a 'user' boundary, skip leading orphan 'tool' messages so the trimmed history never starts with a tool reply lacking its assistant tool_call.
Truncation marker (original_chars=N) tells the model the content was edited rather than silently lying about a short result; UTF-8-safe via .chars().take().
compact's change-guard (compress>0 || dropped>0) makes a no-op compact a true no-op — log stays byte-identical, verified by a test.

Adjacent integrity machinery: backfill_unanswered_tool_calls and sanitize_restored_messages synthesize placeholder tool replies for dangling tool_calls so interrupted/resumed sessions remain valid; log redacts inline base64 images.
tradeoffs_or_gotchas: Char-count budget is a proxy for tokens — it can over- or under-estimate real token usage depending on language/JSON overhead; there is no tokenizer in the loop.

Compression only applies to 'tool' messages whose content is a plain string; multimodal/array tool content or large assistant/user messages are never shrunk by compress_tool_result (only droppable via prefix-cut).

If the recent window (keep_recent_messages) itself exceeds max_chars, the prefix-drop guard body.len() > keep_recent_messages can leave the view over budget — the policy never trims within the kept tail, so the budget is soft, not hard.
Pass 2 recomputes total_chars only against post-compression body; the check uses self.system + notes too, so a large system prompt counts against the budget but is never dropped.

compact rewrites the whole JSONL via truncate+write; on resume the original verbose tool outputs are gone for good (the non-destructive view did not have this consequence). The marker text is the only record of what was cut.
positive_usize fallback means a config of 0 (e.g. someone trying to disable keep-recent) silently reverts to the default 30/4000 rather than behaving as 0.
Counting edited_chars by re-serializing every message on each turn is O(total history size) work per model call — fine at these scales but it is not incremental.

one_liner: A single-threaded tool subsystem where every agent capability implements one `?Send` async `Tool` trait, lives in a `ToolRegistry` over a cheaply-cloned `ToolContext`, and is exposed to the model through a dynamically-pruned, lexically-scored schema view with genome-overridable descriptions and pre/post hook wrapping.
how_it_works: Each capability is a unit struct implementing `trait Tool` (`tools.rs:159`), which the model sees as one OpenAI function tool: `name()`, `description()`, `parameters()` (JSON Schema), a defaulted `read_only()` returning false, and `async fn execute(&self, ctx: &ToolContext, args: &Value) -> String`. The trait is `#[async_trait(?Send)]` because the whole REPL runs on a current-thread runtime, so shared mutable state (the plan, the tool catalog/hints) uses `Rc<RefCell<…>>` rather than `Arc<Mutex<…>>`. `ToolContext` (`tools.rs:55`) is a `Clone` bag of everything a tool needs — workspace, `SandboxPolicy`, approval policy string, timeout, the shared plan, an optional `Rc<dyn ApprovalHandler>`, optional `MemoryStore`, search backend config, the `tool_catalog`, `tool_hints`, hooks, skills, and the `Genome` — built up via `with_*` builder methods. `ToolRegistry::new` (`tools.rs:194`) registers the core set (read_file, apply_patch, update_plan, shell, grep, glob, web_search, web_fetch, tool_search) and conditionally `remember` (only if `ctx.memory.is_some()`) and `skill` (only if skills were discovered) — capability-gating so the model never sees a tool that can't function. On `register` (`tools.rs:229`) the registry computes the effective description via `genome.describe(name, tool.description())` and pushes a `ToolCatalogEntry{name, description, read_only}`; that catalog is what `tool_search` scores, so search sees the same text the model sees. Schema exposure is dynamic: `schemas_limited_for_query` (`tools.rs:283`) returns every tool's schema if the count is ≤ `DEFAULT_VISIBLE_TOOL_LIMIT` (9), otherwise it always includes `ALWAYS_VISIBLE_TOOLS` (read_file, apply_patch, update_plan, shell, tool_search, skill), adds any names recorded in `tool_hints` (set last turn by `tool_search`), then fills the remaining budget with the best lexical matches of the user's query (`catalog_score`), and renders each via `schema_for` (which re-applies the genome override). `execute` (`tools.rs:327`) wraps the call: it runs pre_tool hooks (a block short-circuits with an error string), runs the tool, runs post_tool hooks, and appends any hook stdout under a `[hook output]` banner. The loop (`agent_loop.rs:300,392`) calls `schemas_for_query(user_prompt)` each iteration and uses `is_read_only` to batch consecutive read-only calls for concurrent execution.
design_rationale: The `?Send` trait + `Rc<RefCell>` choice is forced by the current-thread runtime: a `Send` bound would demand `Arc<Mutex>` everywhere and buy nothing, since there is no thread to send to. Dynamic schema exposure exists because exposing every tool every turn wastes prompt tokens and degrades model tool-selection as the registry grows (MCP tools, skills, search); the constant `ALWAYS_VISIBLE_TOOLS` guarantees the irreplaceable core (you can always read, patch, plan, run shell, search for more tools, and load a skill) stays present, and `tool_search` provides the escape hatch — its results become `tool_hints` that surface the matched schemas next turn. The genome description-override path is deliberately a pure text-substitution surface: the training harness (ncx-forge) can evolve descriptions and the base prompt but never tool *behavior*, because the sandbox still governs execution — this keeps a candidate genome from injecting new capability and makes a failed load a guaranteed no-op (empty Genome → byte-identical schemas, asserted by a test). `schema_for` is a registry method distinct from the trait's `to_schema()` so the model-facing schema can carry the override while the trait keeps returning its unmodified default. The `read_only()` default of false is fail-safe: an unclassified tool is treated as a side-effecting write, never auto-batched concurrently. Conditional registration of `remember`/`skill` avoids advertising dead capabilities. The apply_patch description is verbatim load-bearing: trimming it makes the model emit git/unified-diff syntax the V4A parser rejects, looping the turn.

one_liner: Two orthogonal, pure-decision layers — SandboxPolicy (what's physically allowed: reads/writes/network) and Approver (what to do when an action exceeds the sandbox: AutoApprove/Ask/AutoDeny under four approval policies) — with all enforcement and prompting deliberately pushed to consumer crates.
how_it_works: `SandboxPolicy` (policy.rs) holds a `mode` string (one of `read-only`/`workspace-write`/`danger-full-access`), a normalized `workspace` PathBuf, extra `writable_roots`, `network_access`, and an opt-in `allow_temp_write` flag. `can_read` unconditionally returns `true` for all three modes (secret-file protection is left to the tool layer). `can_write` short-circuits: `true` for danger-full-access, `false` for read-only; otherwise it makes the target absolute against the workspace, lexically normalizes it, and returns true iff it `starts_with` any directory in `writable_dirs()` (workspace + writable_roots + system temp only if `allow_temp_write`). Path comparison is purely lexical via `normalize` (drops `.`, pops on `..`, never touches the filesystem) so a decision never depends on a path existing. The `Approver` (approval.rs) is a thin wrapper over a `policy` string; its `classify(command, needs_escalation)` returns a `Decision` enum: `never` -> AutoDeny if escalation needed else AutoApprove; `on-request` -> Ask if escalation needed else AutoApprove; `on-failure` -> always AutoApprove (run sandboxed first, ask only after a failure, handled upstream); `untrusted` -> AutoApprove only if `is_trusted(command)` AND no escalation, else Ask. `is_trusted` first rejects any `dangerous_patterns` regex match (rm -rf, dd, mkfs, fork bombs, etc.), then checks the first token (path-stripped, `.exe`-stripped) against `TRUSTED_COMMANDS`, and for `git` further rejects write subcommands in `GIT_WRITE_SUBCMDS`. `step_decision(base, is_write, require_step_approval)` layers per-step confirmation on top: it upgrades an AutoApprove write to Ask when the user disabled auto-approve, but never softens AutoDeny and never downgrades an existing Ask. Crucially, the `needs_escalation` input and the read-only shell heuristic (`looks_read_only`) are NOT in this crate — the consumer `ncx-core` (tools.rs `ShellTool::needs_escalation`) computes escalation from the policy, and `ncx-tools` (detect.rs) owns the conservative read-only classifier.
design_rationale: The central design decision is separating two orthogonal axes (lib.rs docs say so explicitly): the sandbox answers "is this physically allowed?" and the approver answers "what do we do when it isn't?". This mirrors Codex and lets the same policy work under different trust levels without entangling enforcement with prompting. Both layers are intentionally PURE decision functions — no I/O, no UI — because the actual yes/no prompt is an upper-layer concern (CLI=text prompt, GUI=modal round-trip, tests=canned answer), and enforcement (actually applying a patch / spawning a process) lives in the executor/tools crates. Path comparison is lexical rather than canonicalizing/symlink-resolving so that `can_write` is total and deterministic on non-existent paths (you must gate a file you're about to CREATE) — the doc-comment notes this matches the Python side's `Path.resolve(strict=False)`. `allow_temp_write` defaults to false ("tightened default") to close a hole where the workspace itself lives under the system temp dir but a sibling temp file should still be denied. `untrusted`'s allowlist is conservative/read-only-ish and the dangerous-pattern check runs FIRST so a trusted leading token (bare `rm`, or `git clean`) can't smuggle a destructive command past the gate. `step_decision` is monotone toward safety (only ever upgrades approval, never relaxes) so adding per-step confirmation can never make the system less safe.

key_mechanisms.name: Two orthogonal axes (lib.rs)
key_mechanisms.detail: SandboxPolicy = physical permission (can_read/can_write/network); Approver = escalation decision. Both pure; enforcement and prompting live elsewhere (executor/tools crates, CLI/GUI). This split is the whole architecture.

An Approver::new(approval_policy).classify(command, needs_escalation) returns a Decision.

If per-step confirmation is enabled, step_decision(base, is_write, require_step_approval) upgrades an AutoApprove write to Ask (AutoDeny untouched).
AutoApprove -> run sandboxed; Ask -> upper layer prompts the human via an ApprovalRequest (command/reason/cwd/escalated/details); AutoDeny -> refuse and report.

apply_patch (ncx-tools patch.rs:347) stages all hunks in memory and gates every touched path (and any move_to dest) through the can_write closure before writing anything to disk — atomic all-or-nothing.
interview_talking_points: Why two layers? SandboxPolicy answers 'physically allowed?' and Approver answers 'what to do when not?' — orthogonal, both pure, enforcement/prompting pushed out. This is the headline design and is stated verbatim in lib.rs.

Why lexical path normalization instead of canonicalize? Because can_write must work on files that don't exist yet (you gate a create), so it can't depend on the filesystem; it mirrors Python's Path.resolve(strict=False). Trade-off: it does NOT follow symlinks, so symlink-escape is a known limitation pushed to enforcement.
Component-wise starts_with vs string prefix: explained in the code comment — /a/bc is correctly NOT inside /a/b. A naive string-prefix check would be a real escape bug.

allow_temp_write default false: subtle hole — workspace may live under the system temp dir, but a sibling temp file must still be denied unless explicitly opted in. There's a dedicated test for exactly this.
Four approval policies map cleanly: never (deny escalation), on-request (ask, the default), on-failure (run-then-ask-upstream), untrusted (allowlist gate). Unknown policy -> Ask, a safe fallthrough.

Defense ordering in is_trusted: dangerous patterns are checked BEFORE the allowlist, so a trusted leading token (bare rm, git clean) can't bypass — tested by dangerous_pattern_blocks_trusted_leading_token and untrusted_blocks_dangerous_even_if_leading_token_trusted.
step_decision is monotone: it only ever increases approval friction (AutoApprove write -> Ask), never decreases it, and never touches AutoDeny — so per-step confirmation can't reduce safety.

Two DIFFERENT read-only classifiers exist and shouldn't be conflated: approval.rs's TRUSTED_COMMANDS (for the untrusted policy) and ncx-tools detect.rs's looks_read_only (for read-only-mode escalation). Both are conservative allowlists but serve different gates.

needs_escalation is NOT in this crate — it's computed by the consumer from the policy. The sandbox crate stays a pure library of decisions; this is what makes it testable and reusable across CLI/GUI/tests.
apply_patch escalation UX: the ApprovalRequest.details field carries the FULL diff so the human reviews the actual change, not just file names — a deliberate trust-but-show-evidence choice.
tradeoffs_or_gotchas: Lexical-only normalization means symlinks are NOT resolved — a symlink inside the workspace pointing outside would pass can_write. The crate doc frames enforcement as the executor's job, so symlink-escape mitigation is out of scope here.

can_read always returns true in every mode — there is NO read sandboxing at this layer; reading secrets is only prevented (if at all) at the tool layer. Easy to over-assume the sandbox protects reads.

TRUSTED_COMMANDS includes `python`/`python3`/`node` for the untrusted policy, which can execute arbitrary code; note detect.rs explicitly does the opposite (excludes python -c / node -e). The two lists embody different threat assumptions and can surprise.

is_trusted's first-token git-subcommand parsing splits on whitespace; an unquoted executable path containing spaces would split on the space (same as Python shlex behavior) — only space-free path prefixes normalize correctly, as the test comment notes.

on-failure always returns AutoApprove from classify — the 'ask to retry unsandboxed after a sandboxed failure' behavior is entirely upstream; reading classify alone makes on-failure look like it never prompts.

step_decision keys off is_write/WRITE_TOOLS (shell, apply_patch) supplied by the caller; the sandbox crate doesn't itself know which tool is running, so correct per-step gating depends on the consumer passing the right is_write flag.
network_access is a plain field the policy never enforces; even danger-full-access leaves network_access=false unless a caller (load_config) flips it (tested by danger_full_access_allows_everything).

one_liner: A tiered, recursive node-graph that scales effort to task risk — classify(fast) routes to single-run / plan→best-of-N-workers→verify / recursive decompose — spending a cheap+strong model pair's cost savings on structure (parallel attempts, closed verify-retry loops, divide-and-conquer) to raise completion rate.
how_it_works: `Orchestrator::handle` calls `handle_at(task, 0)`, the recursive core (boxed as `LocalBoxFuture` because an `async fn` that recurses into itself would be infinitely sized, and `?Send`/current-thread is preserved). It first runs `classify` — a tool-less `reason(Tier::Fast, CLASSIFY_SYS, ...)` whose text is parsed by `parse_complexity` (substring match on high/simple/medium; anything unclear defaults to Medium, the safe middle). Simple tasks take a single `run(Tier::Fast, WORKER_SYS, ...)` with no plan/verify. Medium runs `pipeline` = `plan(Tier::Main)` then `run_attempts` with `self.cfg.workers` (default 2) fast parallel workers verified on Fast. High, if `depth < cfg.max_depth`, takes `decompose_and_recurse`; otherwise (depth budget spent, or max_depth=0) falls back to `run_attempts` with `high_workers` (default 3) verified on Main. `run_attempts` is the closed loop: it launches N workers via `join_all` of `run_worker(i, n, ...)` futures (each fed the plan plus the prior round's verifier feedback by `build_worker_task`), runs one `reason(verify_tier, VERIFY_SYS, ...)` over all results, and `verdict_passed` passes unless the text contains 'FAIL' (fail-loud). On pass OR when `rounds > max_verify_retries` it parses `BEST:<n>` via `parse_best_worker` (1-based→0-based, clamped), calls `promote_worker(best)`, and `synthesize` returns the best result (annotated '[unverified after retries]' if it never passed); otherwise the verdict text becomes feedback and it loops. `decompose_and_recurse` plans (Main), runs `reason(Tier::Main, DECOMPOSE_SYS, ...)`, `parse_subtasks` (prefers 'SUBTASK:' lines, falls back to numbered/bulleted lists); <2 subtasks is atomic → best-of-N fallback reusing the plan; otherwise it truncates to `max_subtasks` (default 6), runs each subtask SEQUENTIALLY through `handle_at(st, depth+1)` (so each subtask's promoted winner is visible to the next), AND-combines all `verify_passed`, then does one final Main-tier verify over the joined sub-results.
design_rationale: The module docstring states the explicit premise: "The bottleneck for capability is the model, not the harness," so the orchestrator buys reliability with structure rather than a smarter model — it spends a cheap-model's cost savings on parallel attempts, verification, and decomposition. It deliberately accepts a hard ceiling: plan+verify run on Main, so it "cannot exceed the main model's reasoning ceiling" — the gains are completion-rate on simple/medium and divide-and-conquer reach on high. Effort is matched to risk so cheap tasks stay cheap (Simple skips plan/verify entirely; Medium verifies on Fast not Main). The `AgentRunner` trait abstracts every model call so the module is provider-agnostic and unit-testable with a scripted `MockRunner` (no network). The separate `reason()` method exists specifically so the live runner attaches NO tools to classify/plan/decompose/verify nodes — preventing a capable model from starting to *implement* the task during what should be a judgment/planning step (confirmed in runner.rs: `run_in(..., with_tools=false)` builds `ToolRegistry::empty`). Best-of-N over a cheap model is chosen as a cheaper variance-reduction lever than one expensive run. The closed verify→retry loop with feedback is bounded by `max_verify_retries` to cap cost; verdict parsing is intentionally lenient (substring FAIL, lenient SUBTASK/list parsing, clamped BEST) because LLM output format is unreliable and a usable result shouldn't be lost to a formatting miss. `max_subtasks` guards against a model that over-splits (each subtask is its own full pipeline). Recursion depth is capped (`max_depth`, default 1) so high subtasks that re-classify as high don't decompose forever.

key_mechanisms.name: AgentRunner trait (?Send, async_trait)
key_mechanisms.detail: 4 methods — run/reason/run_worker/promote_worker — abstract all model calls so the node graph is provider-agnostic and testable. reason/run_worker/promote_worker have defaults (delegate to run / ignore isolation / no-op) so simple mock or read-only runners need only implement run. ?Send keeps it current-thread.

key_mechanisms.name: Tool-less reasoning nodes (reason())
key_mechanisms.detail: classify/plan/decompose/verify go through reason(), which the LiveRunner overrides to build ToolRegistry::empty(ctx) (with_tools=false). A capable model literally has no tools to call during a judgment step, so it can't begin executing the task while classifying or verifying.

key_mechanisms.name: Best-of-N parallel workers + verifier selection
key_mechanisms.detail: run_attempts spawns N independent worker futures via futures_util::join_all; each is an isolated attempt so parallel execution can't corrupt shared state. VERIFY_SYS asks for PASS/FAIL plus a 'BEST:<n>' line; parse_best_worker turns that into a 0-based index, and only that winner is promoted.

key_mechanisms.name: Closed verify→retry loop
key_mechanisms.detail: On FAIL and within max_verify_retries, the full verdict text is carried into the next round as `feedback` via build_worker_task ('The previous attempt was rejected. Address this feedback:'). verdict_passed is fail-loud: passes unless the verdict contains 'FAIL'.

key_mechanisms.name: Recursive decomposition with sequential promotion
key_mechanisms.detail: High tasks with ≥2 subtasks recurse via handle_at(st, depth+1) SEQUENTIALLY; each subtask promotes its own verifier-chosen winner to the real workspace before the next runs, so subtasks build on committed work without parallel-write collisions. Depth is bounded by max_depth, count by max_subtasks.

key_mechanisms.name: Workspace isolation + promotion (LiveRunner)
key_mechanisms.detail: run_worker copies the workspace to a per-worker temp scratch dir via copy_tree; promote_worker copies the winner's scratch back onto the real workspace then deletes all scratch copies. copy_tree failure falls back to running in the real workspace (no isolation). Recursion is therefore live-safe.

key_mechanisms.name: Lenient parsing throughout
key_mechanisms.detail: parse_complexity (substring, default Medium), parse_subtasks (SUBTASK: prefix then numbered/bulleted fallback via strip_list_marker), parse_best_worker (clamped, defaults to 0) — all tolerate unreliable LLM formatting so a usable result isn't lost.

key_mechanisms.name: Tier mapping (LiveRunner.model_for)
key_mechanisms.detail: Tier::Main → cfg.model (pro); Tier::Fast → cfg.fast_model (flash) with fallback to cfg.model when fast_model is empty. Each node builds a fresh DeepSeekProvider + Session + tool registry (one-shot turn).

flow_steps: handle(task) → handle_at(task, depth=0), boxed as LocalBoxFuture for self-recursion.
classify: reason(Fast, CLASSIFY_SYS) → parse_complexity → Simple | Medium | High (unclear→Medium).
Simple: single run(Fast, WORKER_SYS); verify_passed=true, verify_rounds=0, no plan.
Medium: pipeline = reason(Main, PLAN_SYS) then run_attempts(verify_tier=Fast, n=cfg.workers=2).
High & depth<max_depth: decompose_and_recurse; else (depth exhausted / max_depth=0): run_attempts(verify_tier=Main, n=high_workers=3).
run_attempts loop: spawn N workers via join_all(run_worker(i,n)), each fed plan + prior feedback (build_worker_task).
verify: reason(verify_tier, VERIFY_SYS, build_verify_task) → verdict_passed (true unless 'FAIL').
If pass OR rounds>max_verify_retries: parse_best_worker(BEST:<n>), promote_worker(best), synthesize → OrchestratorOutcome; else feedback=verdict and loop.
decompose_and_recurse: plan(Main) → reason(Main, DECOMPOSE_SYS) → parse_subtasks.
<2 subtasks → atomic best-of-N fallback on Main reusing the plan; >max_subtasks → truncate.
For each subtask sequentially: handle_at(st, depth+1); AND all verify_passed; collect '[subtask]...' result; each promotes its own winner first.
Final: one reason(Main, VERIFY_SYS) over joined sub-results; verify_passed = all_passed && verdict_passed; synthesize_subtasks → OrchestratorOutcome.
interview_talking_points: Core thesis (from the module doc): the model, not the harness, is the capability bottleneck, so the orchestrator trades a cheap model's cost savings for structure (parallelism, verification, decomposition) to raise reliability — and openly admits it cannot exceed the Main model's reasoning ceiling since plan+verify run there.

Effort scales to risk: Simple skips plan AND verify (one fast run); Medium verifies on Fast; High verifies on Main and gets more attempts (high_workers=3 vs workers=2). This is a cost/reliability dial encoded in OrchestratorConfig.

Why a separate reason() method instead of just run(): tool-less nodes. Without it, a capable model handed the classify prompt plus tools might just start editing files. LiveRunner enforces this with ToolRegistry::empty — a clean separation of 'judge/plan' from 'execute'.

Best-of-N + verifier-picks-BEST is variance reduction over a cheap model: cheaper than one expensive run, and the verifier both gates (PASS/FAIL) and selects (BEST:<n>); only the winner's isolated workspace is promoted.
The closed verify→retry loop feeds the verifier's complaint back into the next workers' prompt (bounded by max_verify_retries) — a self-correction loop, not blind resampling.

Recursion safety is the subtle part: subtasks run SEQUENTIALLY, each promoting its winner to the real workspace before the next, so they build on committed work; parallel workers within one attempt are isolated in temp copies (copy_tree) to avoid write collisions. The boxed LocalBoxFuture is required because an async fn can't recurse without indirection.

Defensive LLM-output parsing everywhere: parse_complexity defaults unclear→Medium, verdict_passed is fail-loud, parse_subtasks falls back from SUBTASK: to numbered/bulleted lists, parse_best_worker clamps and defaults to 0 — the design assumes the model will sometimes ignore the format.

Testability: the whole graph is unit-tested with a scripted MockRunner (no network), asserting exact (tier, stage) call counts — e.g. medium = 1 main plan + 2 fast workers + 1 fast verify; the caps (max_depth, max_subtasks) each have a dedicated test.
tradeoffs_or_gotchas: Hard ceiling acknowledged in the doc: plan and verify run on Main, so the orchestrator cannot out-reason the Main model — it only improves completion-rate/reliability and decomposition reach, not raw capability.

Cost can multiply fast: a high task can fan out to (subtasks × per-subtask pipeline × workers × retry-rounds) model calls, plus extra plan/decompose/verify reasoning calls. max_subtasks and max_depth exist precisely to bound this.

verdict_passed uses a naive substring check — any verifier reply containing the literal 'FAIL' (even 'no FAILures') is treated as a failure; conversely a malformed verify that omits FAIL passes. Robustness was traded for simplicity.
parse_complexity checks 'high' before 'simple'/'medium' via substring; a verbose classifier reply mentioning multiple words could misroute, and any unrecognized reply silently becomes Medium.

Workspace isolation depends on copy_tree of the whole tree per worker per round — potentially expensive for large repos; on copy failure it silently falls back to the REAL workspace, which reintroduces the parallel-write collision it was meant to prevent.

Decomposed-path verification only does ONE final Main verify over joined sub-results (verify_rounds hardcoded to 1, no retry loop at that level) and best_worker is forced to 0 — the per-subtask self-correction happens only inside each recursive handle_at, not at the join.

one_liner: A tiny markdown-backed "self-evolution" store (.ncx/memory/LEARNINGS.md) that lets the agent accumulate verified project notes and recall the most relevant ones into the system prompt as leads (not facts), using a lightweight lexical-semantic ranker plus heuristic and LLM-backed near-duplicate consolidation.
how_it_works: `MemoryStore` (memory.rs) wraps a single path `.ncx/memory/LEARNINGS.md` and persists `MemoryEntry { ts: u64, tags: Vec<String>, text: String }` records. Each entry is serialized as a parseable HTML-comment header `<!-- ts:<n> tags:<a,b> -->` followed by the note body; `parse_entries`/`write_all` round-trip this so the file stays human-readable and hand-editable. `remember(text, tags, now)` trims the text, normalizes it (whitespace-collapsed + lowercased via `normalize`), and skips the write if any existing entry normalizes identically (exact-text dedup returns `Ok(false)`); otherwise it appends, sorts by ts ascending, and drops the oldest beyond `MAX_ENTRIES = 200`. `recall(query, max_entries, max_chars)` scores every entry with `semantic_score` and returns a capped bullet block prefixed by `RECALL_HEADER` which explicitly tells the model to treat the notes as leads to verify, not facts. Scoring is a hybrid lexical-semantic sum: query keywords (lowercased, len>=3, deduped by `keywords`, then widened through a hardcoded domain synonym map in `semantic_aliases` via `expanded_keywords`) score +8 if they match a tag, +4 if they appear in the entry text/tags haystack; adjacent-word `phrases` (bigrams) add +6 on substring hit; and a Jaccard overlap of the two word sets adds up to +20 (`jaccard * 20`). Recency is packed into the low 6 digits (`overlap * 1_000_000 + ts.min(999_999)`) so higher ts wins ties, then entries are emitted until either `max_entries` or `max_chars` is hit. `consolidate(threshold)` is a cheap heuristic dedup run at session start: it sorts newest-first, single-link clusters by `jaccard(word_set) >= threshold`, keeps the newest representative of each cluster, re-caps, and is idempotent. `summarize_consolidate(summarizer, threshold)` does the same greedy clustering but for any multi-entry cluster asks the injected `Summarizer` trait (the fast-model `LiveSummarizer` in the CLI) to fold the notes into one concise note, keeping the cluster's newest ts and the union of its tags; if the LLM returns `None`/empty it falls back to keeping the newest entry, matching the heuristic.
design_rationale: The core stance (memory.rs module doc) is that memory is NOT "raised IQ" but accumulated, verified experience recalled as leads — hence the deliberately untrusting `RECALL_HEADER` wording and the `remember` tool description insisting only CONFIRMED facts be stored, keeping the store trustworthy. Plain markdown with a comment-header format was chosen over a database/embedding index so the store is human-readable, hand-editable, git-diffable, and dependency-free — consistent with the project's "tiny, no heavyweight deps" philosophy; the cost is that retrieval is lexical, not vector-semantic. To recover some semantic reach without an embedding model, the author bolts on a small hand-curated synonym map (`semantic_aliases`, e.g. desktop/native/window -> gui,tauri) and phrase/Jaccard signals — a pragmatic middle ground that the test `recall_uses_semantic_aliases_and_tags` locks in (querying "native installer release package" surfaces a Tauri/bundle note). Recency is folded into the integer score via bit-packing rather than a second sort key, giving a stable deterministic single comparator. `now` is passed in by the caller rather than read from the clock inside the store so writes are deterministic and unit-testable. The `Summarizer` trait is `#[async_trait(?Send)]` and dependency-injected so the core crate stays provider-agnostic and single-threaded-friendly (the whole agent is `!Send`/`Rc`-based), with the real LLM call living in the CLI's `LiveSummarizer` (fast model) and tests using a `FixedMerger` mock. Two consolidation paths exist because the heuristic is free and safe to run every startup, while the LLM merge is better-quality but costs a call — so `consolidate` runs unconditionally at session start (runner.rs / main.rs use 0.85) and `summarize_consolidate` is an explicit opt-in subcommand. The hard 200-entry cap plus char-budgeted recall (e.g. 6 entries/3000 chars in the runner) exist because recalled notes are prepended to the system prompt, so unbounded growth would blow the context window.

key_mechanisms.name: Markdown comment-header store format
key_mechanisms.detail: Each entry is `<!-- ts:<epoch> tags:<csv> -->` + body, written by `write_all` and read by `parse_entries`; file is `.ncx/memory/LEARNINGS.md`. Chosen for human-readability/git-diffability over a DB or vector index (zero deps, but only lexical retrieval).

key_mechanisms.name: Exact-text dedup on remember
key_mechanisms.detail: `remember` compares `normalize(text)` (whitespace-collapsed, lowercased) against existing entries; identical-after-normalization returns Ok(false). Test `dedup_skips_identical` confirms '  SAME   fact ' dedups against 'same fact'.

key_mechanisms.name: MAX_ENTRIES cap (200), oldest-dropped
key_mechanisms.detail: After append, entries are sorted by ts ascending and `drain(0..drop)` removes the front (oldest). `cap_drops_oldest` verifies len==200 and all kept ts>=5. Prevents unbounded prompt growth.

key_mechanisms.name: Hybrid lexical-semantic recall score
key_mechanisms.detail: `semantic_score`: tag match +8, text substring +4 per (alias-expanded) keyword, bigram phrase substring +6, plus Jaccard(query,entry word sets)*20. `expanded_keywords` widens via `semantic_aliases` hardcoded synonym map.

key_mechanisms.name: Recency bit-packing tie-break
key_mechanisms.detail: `s = overlap * 1_000_000 + (e.ts.min(999_999))` then descending sort — a single integer comparator where overlap dominates and recency breaks ties without a secondary sort key.

key_mechanisms.name: Leads-not-facts framing
key_mechanisms.detail: RECALL_HEADER literally instructs 'treat as leads, verify before acting'; the `remember` tool description (tools.rs) restricts writes to CONFIRMED notes only. Recall block is appended to the system prompt by `compose_system_prompt`.

key_mechanisms.name: Heuristic consolidate (Jaccard single-link)
key_mechanisms.detail: Newest-first greedy clustering; an entry is a dup if `jaccard(word_set) >= threshold` against any kept representative. Keeps newest of each cluster, re-caps, idempotent (re-run removes 0). Run at every session start at 0.85.

key_mechanisms.name: LLM summarize_consolidate with fallback
key_mechanisms.detail: Same clustering; for clusters of >1 calls injected `Summarizer::merge` to fold into one note (newest ts + union of tags); on None/empty falls back to keeping newest. `LiveSummarizer` uses the fast model with a 'merge into ONE concise note, <=2 sentences' prompt.

key_mechanisms.name: Injected Summarizer trait
key_mechanisms.detail: `#[async_trait(?Send)] trait Summarizer { async fn merge(&self,&[String]) -> Option<String> }` keeps ncx-core provider-agnostic; CLI provides `LiveSummarizer` (DeepSeekProvider, fast_model), tests use `FixedMerger`.

flow_steps: WRITE: model calls `remember` tool (tools.rs RememberTool) with a confirmed note + optional tags; the tool reads SystemTime as `now` and calls `MemoryStore::remember`.

remember trims/normalizes text, returns Ok(false) on empty or exact-normalized duplicate, else pushes a MemoryEntry, sorts by ts, caps to MAX_ENTRIES (drop oldest), and `write_all` re-serializes the whole markdown file.
SESSION START: CLI/GUI construct `MemoryStore::new(workspace/.ncx/memory)` and call `consolidate(0.85)` (idempotent heuristic near-dup merge) to tidy the store cheaply.
RECALL: caller invokes `recall(query, max_entries, max_chars)` — runner uses (6,3000), CLI uses (8,4000), GUI uses ("",8,4000) for pure-recency at session start with no task yet.
recall computes expanded_keywords (with synonym aliases), the query word_set, and bigram phrases, then `semantic_score`s each entry (tags +8 / text +4 / phrase +6 / jaccard*20).
Scores are bit-packed with recency, sorted descending, and emitted as `- <note>` bullets under RECALL_HEADER until max_entries or max_chars is reached (empty string if nothing scores/stored).
INJECT: `compose_system_prompt` appends the recall block (alongside project instructions and skills index) to the system prompt, so notes ride along as leads for the turn.

OPTIONAL DEEP CONSOLIDATION: `summarize-memory` subcommand builds a `LiveSummarizer` (fast model) and calls `summarize_consolidate(&summarizer, 0.85)`, clustering near-dups and LLM-merging each multi-note cluster into one (newest ts + union tags), falling back to newest on merge failure.
interview_talking_points: Framing matters: this is explicitly 'accumulated verified experience recalled as leads,' not a knowledge base treated as ground truth — enforced both at write time (remember tool: CONFIRMED only) and read time (RECALL_HEADER: 'treat as leads, verify before acting').

Deliberately dependency-free: a single hand-editable markdown file with comment headers instead of SQLite/embeddings — fits the 'tiny' philosophy and is git-diffable, at the cost of lexical-only retrieval.
How they fake semantic recall without embeddings: a hand-curated `semantic_aliases` synonym map + bigram phrases + Jaccard word-set overlap, combined into one additive `semantic_score`.
The single-integer scoring comparator: `overlap * 1_000_000 + ts.min(999_999)` packs relevance and recency so one descending sort gives relevance-primary, recency-tiebreak ordering deterministically.
Testability through injected `now`: the store never reads the clock itself, so dedup/cap/recall tests are fully deterministic; the caller (RememberTool) supplies SystemTime.
Two-tier consolidation as a cost/quality tradeoff: free heuristic Jaccard dedup runs every session start (idempotent), while the LLM merge is an explicit, paid opt-in that produces nicer fused notes.

Provider-agnostic core via the `?Send` `Summarizer` trait — ncx-core never imports a model client; the CLI's `LiveSummarizer` wires the fast model in, tests use a mock. Mirrors the project's `!Send`/Rc single-threaded design.
Bounded context safety: 200-entry hard cap + char-budgeted recall block, because recall is prepended to the system prompt every turn.
tradeoffs_or_gotchas: Dedup on remember is EXACT-text only (after normalize); near-duplicates with different wording slip through until a `consolidate`/`summarize_consolidate` pass — dedup and consolidation are intentionally two different similarity bars.
`semantic_aliases` is a tiny hardcoded, domain-specific map (gui/tauri/build/rust/etc.); recall semantics won't generalize beyond this project's vocabulary and must be hand-extended.

Recency packing caps ts contribution at 999_999 (`ts.min(999_999)`), and any score difference of >=1 in overlap (x1_000_000) dominates ts entirely — so recency only ever breaks exact relevance ties, never overrides relevance.
`word_set`/`keywords` drop tokens shorter than 3 chars, so short but meaningful tokens (e.g. 'go', 'ci', 'os') never contribute to Jaccard or keyword matching.
Whole-file rewrite on every successful remember/consolidate (`write_all` serializes all entries) — fine at the 200-cap scale but O(n) per write, not append-only despite the 'append-only-ish' comment.
`recall` scoring substring-matches keywords against the haystack with `hay.contains(w)`, so it can match inside larger words (substring, not word-boundary) — a possible source of spurious +4 hits.

`consolidate` returning removed-count and only writing when removed>0 makes it cheap/idempotent, but it silently keeps the NEWEST of a near-dup cluster, which may discard a better-worded older note in favor of a sloppier recent one (LLM merge exists precisely to mitigate this).

one_liner: Two-tier progressive-disclosure Agent Skills (SKILL.md index always-on, full body fetched via the `skill` tool), MCP server tools wrapped as first-class ncx Tools sharing one Rc<Mutex<McpClient>> with heuristic read-only/approval gating, and per-turn vision routing that diverts image-bearing turns to an optional dedicated vision Provider.
how_it_works: SKILLS: A `Skill` (skills.rs) is a directory holding `SKILL.md` with `---`-fenced YAML frontmatter (`name:`, `description:`). `discover_skills` -> `discover_skills_with_home` seeds a `BTreeMap<String,Skill>` with `builtin_skills()` (compiled in via `include_str!`, currently just `commit-message`), then overlays two filesystem roots in order — `~/.ncx/skills/*` then `<workspace>/.ncx/skills/*` — so later same-name skills shadow earlier ones (workspace beats home beats builtin). `parse_frontmatter`/`frontmatter_lines`/`strip_frontmatter` hand-parse only the two needed keys (no YAML lib); `name` falls back to the directory name. Level-1 disclosure: `skills_index_block` emits only `- name: description` lines under a fixed header into the system prompt (composed in main.rs as `skills_index`, the 3rd extra block). Level-2: the `SkillTool` (tools.rs, `read_only`) is registered ONLY when `ctx.skills` is non-empty; on call it case-insensitively finds the skill and returns `Skill::load_body()` — embedded string for builtins, else `std::fs::read_to_string` + `strip_frontmatter` — prefixed with the skill's directory so the model can `read_file` bundled resources (level 3). MCP: `register_mcp_server` (mcp_tool.rs) does `McpClient::connect` over stdio, `list_tools`, then wraps the single client in `Rc<Mutex<McpClient>>` and registers one `McpTool` per `McpToolDef`, all sharing that handle. `McpTool` implements `Tool` (`?Send`), forwarding name/description/input_schema and computing `read_only` once via `is_read_only_name` (prefix/exact heuristic: read_/get_/list_/fetch_/search_/find_). On `execute`, non-read-only tools first run `Approver::new(&ctx.approval_policy).classify(name, true)`; `AutoDeny` returns an error string, `Ask` calls `ctx.approver.request(...)` with `escalated:true` (denial returns an error, missing approver falls through), `AutoApprove` proceeds; then `client.lock().await` serialises the `call_tool` RPC. VISION: each `run_turn_inner` sets `use_vision_this_turn = vision_provider.is_some() && has_image_block(user_input)`, where `has_image_block` checks the user content array for any block whose `type == "image_url"`. `active_provider()` returns the vision provider for that turn only when both are true, else the main provider; `call_model` calls `.chat` on whichever `active_provider()` returns. The vision provider is an optional `Box<dyn Provider>` built in main.rs by `build_vision_provider` (a `DeepSeekProvider` pointed at `vl_model`/`vl_base_url`/`vl_api_key`, falling back to the main creds when unset; `None` if `vl_model` is empty).
design_rationale: Progressive disclosure exists to keep the always-on prompt cheap: injecting only name+description for every skill (which may bundle large bodies and helper files) avoids paying tokens for instructions the current task doesn't need; the doc comment explicitly frames this as the same two-tier catalog shape as `tool_search`. Builtins via `include_str!` guarantee a baseline skill set with zero filesystem dependency (ships in the single binary), while filesystem shadowing lets users override builtins without recompiling — the BTreeMap insert-order overlay is the cheapest way to express that precedence and also yields deterministic name-sorted output. The hand-rolled frontmatter parser is a deliberate dependency-minimisation choice: only two scalar keys matter, so pulling in a YAML crate would be overkill. For MCP, one `Rc<Mutex<McpClient>>` shared by all of a server's tools is forced by the architecture: the client owns one server process and one stdio JSON-RPC pipe, so concurrent calls MUST be serialised — the Mutex makes interleaved request/response framing impossible to corrupt, and `Rc` (not `Arc`) is correct because the whole agent runs on a current-thread, `!Send` runtime (note the `#[async_trait(?Send)]`). Reusing `ctx.approver`/`Approver`/`Decision` deliberately gives MCP side-effecting tools the exact same escalation model as `ShellTool` rather than inventing a parallel path; the name-prefix read-only heuristic is an admitted approximation (the test comment even flags `echo` as a misclassification edge) chosen because MCP's protocol exposes no machine-readable side-effect flag. Vision routing is per-turn and opt-in: rather than a separate multimodal pipeline or forcing one model to be both coder and vision-capable, image turns transparently divert to a specialised provider while text turns stay on the main coding model, and when no vision provider is configured image turns simply stay on the main provider (graceful no-op). Detection keys on the OpenAI-style `image_url` block so the same `content` array works for both providers.

key_mechanisms.detail: skills_index_block injects only `- name: description` lines (level 1); SkillTool.execute returns the full SKILL.md body + dir on demand (level 2), enabling read_file of bundled resources (level 3). SkillTool is registered only when ctx.skills is non-empty (tools.rs:213-216).

Non-read-only tools run Approver::classify(name,true): AutoDeny->error, Ask->ctx.approver.request(escalated:true), AutoApprove->proceed — identical to ShellTool (mcp_tool.rs:38-46,66-104).
